injunction

/in-JUNGK-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Injunction means an official court order requiring someone to do something or, more often, to stop doing it.

The judge issued an injunction forbidding the startup from using its rival's secret formula while the lawsuit continued.

Example

For months, the residents of Milbrook watched gray foam drift down the river behind the chemical plant. Independent tests showed the plant was releasing waste far above legal limits. The town sued, and the judge granted an injunction ordering the plant to halt all discharges immediately. Until the case is resolved, the plant cannot release a single gallon into the river.

The court order forcing the plant to stop its discharges is an injunction, a legal command to stop a specific action.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

court order: A court order is any official command a judge issues — to pay damages or hand over documents. An injunction is one specific kind of court order: it requires a party to do something or, more often, to stop doing it, usually while a case is decided. Every injunction is a court order; most court orders are not injunctions.

prohibition: A prohibition is an order forbidding an action, and it can come from any authority — a legislature, an agency, a landlord — as a standing rule. An injunction comes only from a court, binds the specific parties in a live dispute, and usually lasts until the case ends. A prohibition sets a standing rule; an injunction polices one dispute.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

permission: official consent to do something

Where it sits · how binding and lasting the stop is — request → injunction → ban

request vs. injunction: A request politely asks someone to stop an activity, while an injunction legally compels them to stop.

ban vs. injunction: An injunction usually pauses an activity while a case is decided, while a permanent ban ends the activity for good.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: on, upon

Root — junct

Root — junct: from Latin iungere, to join

Suffix — -ion

Suffix — -ion: the act or result of

Put it together

Put it together: From Latin in-, meaning on or upon, plus iungere, meaning to join, giving injungere, to impose upon. An injunction is literally an order joined onto someone by legal authority.

Use the root in a new word: conjunction

Use the root in a new word: conjunction: In grammar, a conjunction such as the word and joins two parts of a sentence together.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal, legal register

Injunction appears almost exclusively in legal contexts, usually with verbs like issue, grant, or seek. Courts most often use injunctions to stop an activity temporarily while a lawsuit is being decided.
